w: Its rose window spans nearly 14 metres, the second-largest surviving Gothic rose window anywhere; the nave rises 44 metres, the eighth-highest in the world. Known as La Seu, it rose on a former mosque site after the 1229 reconquest, finished by the 17th century, abutting the old city walls beside the Royal Palace.
s: Gothic cathedral with the world's second-largest rose window
_facts: Rose window nearly 14m diameter, second-largest extant Gothic rose window
44m-high nave, eighth-highest in the world
Built on former mosque site, begun after the 1229 reconquest, finished 17th century
Sits between the Royal Palace of La Almudaina and the Episcopal Palace

w: One of only a handful of circular castles left in Europe, raised in the 14th century on a hill above Palma for King James II of Majorca. It served as a royal residence, then a military prison from the 18th into the mid-20th century, and now houses the city's History Museum.
s: Rare circular Gothic castle, once a royal prison
_facts: Built 14th century for King James II of Majorca
One of the few circular castles in Europe
Used as a military prison from the 18th to mid-20th century
Now houses Palma's History Museum

w: Originally an Arab fortress, remodelled at the start of the 14th century into a residence for the kings of Majorca. Standing directly opposite Palma Cathedral, La Almudaina remains one of the official residences of the Spanish royal family today, though Marivent now hosts them for the summer.
s: Arab fortress rebuilt into a Spanish royal palace
_facts: Originally an Arab fortress
Major remodelling at the start of the 14th century
Located directly opposite Palma Cathedral
Still one of the official Spanish royal residences

w: Built in the 1920s in Cala Mayor, Marivent has been the Spanish royal family's summer residence since the 1970s and is said to be Queen Sofia's favourite. Unlike the official Almudaina palace, it belongs to the Balearic government, not the Patrimonio Nacional, and has hosted meetings with Spain's prime minister.
s: 1920s palace, Spanish royals' summer home since the 70s
_facts: Built in the 1920s in Cala Mayor
Summer residence of the Spanish royal family since the 1970s
Owned by the Balearic government, not the Patrimonio Nacional
Used for royal receptions with the Spanish prime minister and foreign leaders

w: Joan Miro and his wife Pilar Juncosa founded this Palma museum in 1981, donating 6,000 works. It preserves his studios Son Boter, bought in 1959, and the larger atelier designed by Josep Lluis Sert, used until Miro's death in 1983. Rafael Moneo's 1992 building added exhibition space alongside the sculpture garden.
s: Joan Miro's studios and his 6,000-work gift to Palma
_facts: Founded 1981 by Joan Miro and Pilar Juncosa
6,000 works donated by the artist
Preserves Miro's studios Son Boter and the Sert-designed atelier
1992 museum building designed by Rafael Moneo

w: Palma's museum of modern and contemporary art opened on 30 January 2004 with a reserve of more than 700 works tied to Balearic and international artists. The founding collection came from the Art Serra Foundation plus Palma City Council, the Council of Mallorca and the Balearic government.
s: Palma's modern art museum, 700-plus works since 2004
_facts: Opened 30 January 2004
Reserve of 700+ works linked to Balearic and international artists
Founding collection from the Art Serra Foundation and public bodies
Runs temporary exhibitions and educational programmes

w: This former hotel on Plaza Weyler, in the heart of Palma's historic centre, stopped taking guests and reopened in 1993 as a CaixaForum, one venue in the banking group La Caixa's chain of art spaces. The Gran Hotel name has stuck to the building ever since, even though its trade shifted from beds to exhibitions.
s: Former hotel on Plaza Weyler, now an art venue
_facts: Former historic hotel on Plaza Weyler
Part of Palma's historic centre
Reopened as a CaixaForum in 1993
Run by banking group La Caixa's art-venue chain

w: The Porto Pi Lighthouse is one of the oldest operating lighthouses anywhere, still marking the entrance to Palma harbour on the island of Majorca. Its age and long service at the harbour mouth have earned it protection as a historic monument, a rare working survivor among lighthouses of its vintage.
s: One of the oldest working lighthouses in the world
_facts: One of the oldest operating lighthouses in the world
Marks the entrance to Palma harbour
Protected as a historic monument

w: Palma's oldest local library sits inside the town council's own Cort building, at Cort square 1, and belongs to the Bibliopalma network. Beyond lending books, it runs exhibitions, presentations, conferences and reading clubs, with holdings searchable online via the Balearic bibliographic catalogue.
s: Palma's oldest library, tucked inside the town hall
_facts: Oldest of Palma's local libraries
Housed inside the town council building at Cort square 1
Part of the Bibliopalma network
Hosts exhibitions, presentations, conferences and reading clubs

w: Built in 1910 for the Balearic Regional Exhibition, this roughly 500-metre seafront street runs from Avinguda Antonio Maura and the Muelle Viejo to the Riera torrent. It takes its name from Guillem Sagrera, the Gothic architect whose building on the street -- the Llotja, Palma's old merchants' exchange -- still stands today.
s: 1910 exhibition-era promenade named for its Gothic architect
_facts: Built in 1910 for the Balearic Regional Exhibition
About 500 metres long, from Av. Antonio Maura/Muelle Viejo to the Riera torrent
Named for architect Guillem Sagrera
